name: Portfolio Optimisation Beyond Mean and Variance
title: Portfolio Optimisation Beyond Mean and Variance
answer: Portfolio optimisation beyond mean and variance covers methods that go past expected return and variance as the only summary of a portfolio. It includes higher moments such as skewness and kurtosis, downside measures such as semivariance, value at risk, expected shortfall and maximum drawdown, and dependence structures that capture tail co-movement. For AI-related instruments the scope also includes event risk from litigation, regulation and product cycles, because these can create fat tails and regime shifts that a two-moment model misses. The field sits in portfolio construction and draws on statistics, optimisation and machine learning, but the output is still a set of weights and constraints rather than a prediction of individual prices.

sections.body: Portfolio optimisation beyond mean and variance covers methods that go past expected return and variance as the only summary of a portfolio. It includes higher moments such as skewness and kurtosis, downside measures such as semivariance, value at risk, expected shortfall and maximum drawdown, and dependence structures that capture tail co-movement. For AI-related instruments the scope also includes event risk from litigation, regulation and product cycles, because these can create fat tails and regime shifts that a two-moment model misses. The field sits in portfolio construction and draws on statistics, optimisation and machine learning, but the output is still a set of weights and constraints rather than a prediction of individual prices.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a data pipeline that ingests daily prices for the 117 listed AI-related instruments the site tracks, along with fundamentals, filings, news and alternative data. Compute is typically split between CPUs for data preparation and optimisation and GPUs for heavier estimation tasks such as deep learning or large-scale scenario generation. Common tools include Python and R, with libraries such as NumPy, pandas and scikit-learn for data handling and modelling, and solvers such as CVXPY or commercial optimisers for the final allocation problem. Backtesting engines, version-controlled notebooks and reproducible data snapshots are part of the infrastructure because results must be auditable.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The method starts by choosing an objective that reflects the risk the portfolio is meant to control, for example maximising expected return subject to an expected shortfall limit or minimising drawdown under a return target. Inputs are estimated with factor models, Bayesian shrinkage, copulas or machine learning models that capture non-normal dependence and time-varying volatility. The optimisation itself may use convex programming, stochastic programming, robust optimisation or reinforcement learning, depending on the objective and constraints. Practitioners then run walk-forward backtests with realistic transaction costs, turnover limits and liquidity constraints, and they compare results against simpler mean-variance benchmarks to see whether the added complexity earns its keep.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Governance covers data rights, model risk and provenance. Data must be licensed for the intended use, and the pipeline must record where each price, filing or news item came from so that results can be reproduced and audited. Model risk is high because higher-moment and tail estimates are sensitive to outliers, regime changes and overfitting, so validation often includes stress tests and out-of-sample checks. For AI-related portfolios, the site tracks 148 active AI lawsuits and 219 compliance and regulation pages, which can feed event-risk indicators and help document why certain constraints exist. Fiduciary duties and regulatory rules may limit the use of complex models if they cannot be explained to clients or supervisors.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The horizon points toward more integrated risk models that combine market, litigation and regulatory signals in one optimisation framework. Machine learning is likely to play a larger role in estimating tail dependence and regime shifts, while explainability and reproducibility will remain requirements rather than optional extras. Multi-period and robust methods are gaining ground because single-period mean-variance models struggle with path-dependent risks such as drawdown and liquidity. For AI-related portfolios, concentration and event risk may keep pushing practitioners toward tail-aware and scenario-based approaches, even as the underlying optimisation problems become harder to solve.
